title: Corporate headshots when your team is in 40 states
summary: Corporate headshots now happen one person at a time in hundreds of cities. Snappr booking data shows what replaced the company photo day.
body_markdown:
## The photo day is less than 1% of the work


*One doctor, one clinic, one session. That is over 90% of corporate headshot bookings.*


Someone on your ops team books the conference room. Thursday, ten-minute slots, a sign-up sheet in Slack. The photographer arrives with two lights and a grey backdrop. By 4:15 it is done, and forty-one people have a new photo.


Eleven people do not. They live in Boise, Tampa, Fort Wayne and eight other places nobody flew to. Two more start in three weeks. One just got promoted and needs a version without the old office wall in it.


That gap is not an edge case anymore. It is the job.


Snappr's 2025 and 2026 booking data shows 93.6% of corporate headshot sessions are a single person, in a single city, on a single day. The classic photo day, five or more people at one location on one date, is 0.3% of volume.


The reason is structural. Gallup found that among remote-capable US employees, 52% work hybrid and 28% are exclusively remote, leaving 21% fully on-site. A photo day only captures whoever happens to be in the building.


## What replaced it: one person, one city, every week


*Same white backdrop, any city. That is what writing the spec once actually buys you.*


Since January 2024, Snappr has delivered enterprise headshots in over 800 distinct US counties. In 300 of them, exactly one person was ever photographed. Roughly 69% of the volume lands outside the twenty largest counties, where no headshot studio exists and a fly-in photographer will never clear the travel cost for one subject.


These programs also do not stop. One of our clients booked headshots in 114 of the last 115 weeks, across 287 cities in 43 states. Another ran 1,330 sessions across 358 cities in 49 states, active every single week they have been a customer. That is not an annual refresh. It is onboarding.


The trigger is usually a hire. BLS data puts median employee tenure at 3.9 years, the lowest since 2002, so a 400-person company is replacing roughly two people a week, forever. One 2026 industry survey found 1 in 3 headshot refreshes is triggered by a single new hire.


## Consistency is the thing that actually breaks


*Neutral wall, even light, one crop. Write it down once and Boise matches Manhattan.*


When one person books their own session in Boise, the result is a photograph. It is rarely the same photograph your other 400 people have.


Backdrop drifts from grey to white to a lobby plant. Crop moves from mid-chest to shoulders. One vendor delivers warm, another cool. Six months of local bookings and your leadership page reads as a collage. When we ranked[the Fortune 500 CEOs with the best and worst headshots](https://www.snappr.com/blog/the-fortune-500-ceos-with-the-best-and-worst-headshots) , the worst offenders were almost never badly lit. They were mismatched.


Price variance compounds it. HeadShots Inc puts the market range at $89 to $1,500 per person depending on geography and provider. Let 40 locations each source their own and you are paying seventeen rates for seventeen looks.


## Run a program, not an event


Four things separate a headshot program from a scramble.


• Write the spec once. Backdrop color, crop ratio, lighting setup, retouch level, file naming. Every photographer in every market shoots to the same sheet.


• Make booking self-serve. If the new hire in Tampa has to email facilities, the photo happens in month four, or never.


• Set a trigger, not a calendar. Day 14 of onboarding beats 'sometime next spring.'


• Centralize delivery. Photos land in one library, tagged to the person, ready for the directory and the CRM.


The hard part is not writing the standard. It is having a vetted photographer within driving distance of Fort Wayne on a Tuesday, and the same one available six weeks later. Most companies solve this by shrinking the standard to fit the vendors they can find, which is how[image quality and consistency quietly become a brand problem](https://www.snappr.com/blog/image-quality-and-consistency-are-key-factors-in-determining-success-for-leading-brands-in-real-estate) .


## How this runs at Snappr scale


Snappr's photographer network covers 95% of US geography, which turns the one-person-in-Boise booking into a routine transaction rather than a project. Sessions book in about two minutes with 24 hours' notice, because hiring rarely gives more warning.


The shoot spec is set at the account level and applied in every market, so Fort Wayne is shot to the same brief as Manhattan. Editing runs centrally rather than through each local shooter, and photos come back tagged and ready for your directory or HRIS. Healthcare leans on this hardest: clinician networks are 60% of Snappr's enterprise headshot volume, because provider directories need a current photo of every doctor, and doctors sit one per clinic across dozens of states. The full setup is on the[business portraits page](https://www.snappr.com/use-cases/business-portraits) .


If your team is spread across more states than you have offices,[book time with Snappr's Enterprise team](https://www.snappr.com/enterprise) to map out a standing headshot program.


## Frequently asked questions


### How do you get consistent corporate headshots across multiple states?


Lock the specification before you book anyone. Define backdrop, crop, lighting, retouch level and file naming in one document, then require every photographer to shoot to it and route all editing through a single team. Consistency comes from a fixed brief and centralized post-production, not from using the same photographer everywhere.


### Is it cheaper to fly one photographer to every office?


Only when your people sit in a handful of offices. Snappr data shows 93.6% of enterprise headshot sessions are a single person in a single city, and travel cost per subject makes fly-in coverage impractical at that shape.


### How often should corporate headshots be refreshed?


Tie it to headcount change instead of the calendar. With median US tenure at 3.9 years, a rolling new-hire trigger keeps a directory current far better than a company-wide re-shoot.


### What about remote employees who never visit an office?


They book a local session near home, usually within 24 hours' notice. In Snappr's network that is the majority case rather than the exception, with sessions delivered across 889 US counties since January 2024.
